'''East Harlem''', also known as '''Spanish Harlem''' or '''{{lang|es|El Barrio}}''', and formerly '''Italian Harlem''', is a [[neighborhood]] of [[Upper Manhattan]] in [[New York City]], north of the [[Upper East Side]] and bounded by [[96th Street (Manhattan)|98th Street]] to the south, [[Fifth Avenue]] to the west, and the [[East River|East]] and [[Harlem River]]s to the east and north.<ref name=enc-nyc/><ref name=hot/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nyc.com/visitor_guide/el_barrio_spanish_harlem.75851/editorial_review.aspx |title=El Barrio (Spanish Harlem) New York City.com : Visitor Guide : Editorial Review |publisher=Nyc.com |access-date=September 19, 2012}}</ref> Despite its name, it is generally not considered to be a part of [[Harlem|Harlem proper]], but it is one of the neighborhoods included in Greater Harlem.<ref>[[Jeffrey S. Gurock|Gurock, Jeffrey S.]], et al. "Harlem" in {{cite enc-nyc2}}, p. 573.</ref>

The neighborhood has one of the largest [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Hispanic]] communities in New York City, mostly [[Puerto Ricans]], as well as [[Dominican Americans|Dominican]]s, [[Salvadoran Americans|Salvadorans]], [[Cuban Americans|Cuban]]s, and [[Mexicans]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Exploring the Latino Metropolis: East Harlem |url=https://scalar.usc.edu/works/latino-metropolis-a-brief-urban-cultural-history-of-us-latinos---1/east-harlem-1 |access-date=2026-04-13 |website=Exploring the Latino Metropolis: A Brief Urban Cultural History of US Latinos |language=en}}</ref> The community is notable for its contributions to [[Latin freestyle]] and [[salsa music]]. East Harlem also includes the remnants of a once-predominant [[Italian Americans|Italian community]], or Italian Harlem. The [[Chinese in New York City|Chinese]] population has increased dramatically in East Harlem since 2000.<ref name="Mays 2011"/><ref name="Barron 2013"/><ref name="APA 2012"/>

East Harlem has historically suffered from many social issues, such as a high crime rate, the highest [[unemployment|jobless rate]] in New York City, [[teenage pregnancy]], [[AIDS]], [[drug abuse]], [[homelessness]], and an [[asthma]] rate five times the national average.<ref name="nyc.gov">{{cite web |url=http://www.nyc.gov/html/dcp/pdf/pub/mnneeds_2012.pdf |title=Community District Needs |access-date=September 19, 2012 |website=[[Government of New York City]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130317001127/http://www.nyc.gov/html/dcp/pdf/pub/mnneeds_2012.pdf |archive-date=March 17, 2013}}</ref> It has the second-highest concentration of [[public housing in the United States]], behind [[Brownsville, Brooklyn]].<ref name="Mays 2011 2"/> East Harlem is undergoing some [[gentrification]], and in 2016 the city considered rezoning the area.

East Harlem is part of [[Manhattan Community Board 11|Manhattan Community District 11]], and its primary ZIP Codes are 10029 and 10035.<ref name="NYCPlanning"/> It is patrolled by the 23rd and 25th Precincts of the [[New York City Police Department]].<ref name="NYPD 25th Precinct"/><ref name="NYPD 23rd Precinct"/>

==History==
{{see also|History of Harlem}}

===Early history===
[[File:IRT Lexington Avenue Line a8e3c4b09d o.jpg|thumb|First earth from Lexington Avenue subway line in 1913]]
The area that became East Harlem was rural for most of the 19th century, but residential settlements northeast of [[Third Avenue]] and [[110th Street (Manhattan)|East 110th Street]] had developed by the 1860s.<ref name=enc-nyc/> The construction of the [[rapid transit|elevated transit line]] to Harlem in 1879 and 1880, and the building of the [[IRT Lexington Avenue Line|Lexington Avenue subway]] in 1919,<ref name=enc-nyc /> urbanized the area, precipitating the construction of apartment buildings and [[brownstone]]s. The extension of cable cars up Lexington Avenue into East Harlem was stymied by the incline created by [[Duffy's Hill]] at [[103rd Street (Manhattan)|103rd Street]], one of the steepest grades in Manhattan. East Harlem was first populated by poor German, Irish, Scandinavian,<ref name=aia /> and [[Eastern European]] [[Jews in New York City|Jewish]] immigrants, with the Jewish population standing at 90,000 around 1917.<ref name=enc-nyc /> In the 1870s, Italian immigrants joined the mix after a contractor building trolley tracks on First Avenue imported Italian laborers as [[strikebreaker]]s. The workers' [[shantytown]] along the East River at 106th Street was the beginning of an Italian neighborhood, with 4,000 having arrived by the mid-1880s. As more immigrants arrived, it expanded north to [[115th Street (Manhattan)|East 115th Street]] and west to [[Third Avenue (Manhattan)|Third Avenue]].<ref name=gotham1123>{{cite gotham}}, p.1123-24</ref>

East Harlem consisted of pockets of ethnically sorted settlements – Italian, German, Irish, and Jewish – which were beginning to press up against each other, with the spaces still between them occupied by "gasworks, stockyards and tar and garbage dumps".<ref name=gotham1123 /> In 1895, the [[Union Settlement Association]], one of the oldest settlement houses in New York City, began providing services in the area, offering the immigrant and low-income residents a range of community-based programs, including boys and girls clubs, a sewing school and adult education classes.

===Italian Harlem===
{{multiple image
|align=right
|direction=horizontal
|header=Vestiges of Italian Harlem
|image1=Lady Mt Carmel RCC sunny jeh.jpg
|width1=195
|caption1=[[Church of Our Lady of Mount Carmel (Manhattan)|Church of Our Lady of Mount Carmel]]

[[Southern Italy|Southern Italians]] and [[Sicilian people|Sicilians]], with a moderate number of [[North Italy|Northern Italians]], soon predominated, especially in the area east of [[Lexington Avenue (Manhattan)|Lexington Avenue]] between [[96th Street (Manhattan)|96th]] and [[116th Street (Manhattan)|116th]] Streets and east of [[Madison Avenue]] between 116th and [[125th Street (Manhattan)|125th]] Streets, with each street featuring people from different regions of Italy. The neighborhood became known as "Italian Harlem", the [[Italian American]] hub of Manhattan; it was the first part of Manhattan to be referred to as "[[Little Italy, Manhattan|Little Italy]]".<ref>{{cite inside}} p.154</ref> The first Italians arrived in East Harlem in 1878, from [[Polla, Italy|Polla]] in the province of [[Salerno]], and settled in the vicinity of 115th Street.<ref name="meyer">{{Cite web |last=Meyer |first=Gerald |url=http://vitomarcantonio.com/east-harlem/italian-east-harlem/ |title=Italian Harlem: America's Largest and Most Italian Little Italy |website=vitomarcantonio.com |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140812211625/http://vitomarcantonio.com/east-harlem/italian-east-harlem/ |archive-date=August 12, 2014 }}</ref>

[[File:Black Hand Wanted Poster.jpg|thumb|220px|left|A New York Police Department wanted poster for [[Black Hand (extortion)|Black Hand]] activity, 1910]]
There were many [[crime syndicate]]s in Italian Harlem, from the early [[Black Hand (extortion)|Black Hand]] to the bigger and more organized Italian gangs that formed the [[Italian-American Mafia]]. It was the founding location of the [[Genovese crime family]], one of the [[Five Families]] that dominated organized crime in New York City.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://americanmafiahistory.com/genovese-family/ |title=Genovese Crime Family-One of the "Five Families" |publisher=American Mafia History |date=May 6, 2012 |access-date=September 19, 2012}}</ref> This includes the current [[116th Street Crew]] of the Genovese family. During the 1970s, Italian East Harlem was also home to the Italian-American drug gang and murder-for-hire crew known as the [[East Harlem Purple Gang]].

In the 1920s and early 1930s, Italian Harlem was represented in Congress by future Mayor [[Fiorello H. La Guardia]].<ref name=enc-nyc/> After becoming mayor, La Guardia helped plan a large expansion of [[Thomas Jefferson Park]] at First Avenue, between 111th and 114th Streets, in the mid-1930s.<ref>{{cite web |title=Thomas Jefferson Park Highlights |url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/thomas-jefferson-park/history |access-date=January 11, 2021 |publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation}}</ref> The neighborhood was represented, in the 1940s, by Italian-American civil rights lawyer, [[socialism|socialist]], and activist [[Vito Marcantonio]]. The Italian neighborhood approached its peak in the 1930s, with more than 110,000 Italian-Americans living in its crowded, run-down apartment buildings.<ref name=enc-nyc>Lapp, Michael "East Harlem" in {{cite enc-nyc2|page=391}} Quote: "During the 1930s as many as 110,000 Italians lived east of Lexington Avenue between 96th and 116th streets and east of Madison Avenue between 116th and 125th streets."</ref> The 1930 census showed that 81 percent of the population of Italian Harlem consisted of first- or second-generation Italian Americans, somewhat less than the concentration of Italian Americans in the [[Lower East Side]]'s [[Little Italy, Manhattan|Little Italy]] with 88 percent; Italian Harlem's total population, however, was three times that of Little Italy.<ref name=meyer/>

The character of the Italian-American community changed when, after the Second World War, the unhealthy tenements started to be demolished and replaced with better housing, forcing families to relocate. Despite this, Italian Harlem endured as a large and conspicuous community through the 1980s and 1990s, and even later, the Italian-American community in East Harlem remained strong in certain areas, particularly around [[Pleasant Avenue]].

Today, the few remaining Italian-American residents in Harlem are predominantly older, clustered around [[Pleasant Avenue]] and the [[Church of Our Lady of Mt. Carmel (Manhattan)|Our Lady of Mount Carmel Church]], mainly from [[114th Street (Manhattan)|114th]] to [[118th Street (Manhattan)|118th]] Streets and the surrounding area. According to the [[2000 United States census|2000 Census]], there were only 1,130 Italian-Americans still living in this area.<ref>Garland, Sarah. [https://www.nytimes.com/2006/09/05/nyregion/05festival.html?_r=1&oref=slogin "A Reunion of Little Italy in East Harlem"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170730072429/http://www.nytimes.com/2006/09/05/nyregion/05festival.html?_r=1&oref=slogin |date=July 30, 2017 }}, ''The New York Times'', September 5, 2006. Accessed January 2, 2008. "Now, there are only 1,130 Italian-Americans left in East Harlem, according to the 2000 census."</ref>

However, vestiges of the old Italian neighborhood remain. The annual Feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel and the "Dancing of the Giglio", the first Italian feast in New York City, is still celebrated there every year on the second weekend of August by the [[Giglio Society of East Harlem]] and is centered around Church of Our Lady of Mount Carmel. Italian retail establishments still exist in Italian Harlem, such as [[Rao's]] restaurant, which started in 1896, and the original [[Patsy's Pizzeria]], which opened in 1933. Another major Italian retail business in the neighborhood, a barbershop opened by Claudio Caponigro on 116th Street in the mid-1950s,<ref name="Berger">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/11/11/nyregion/sit-this-chair-go-back-time-barber-unchanged-old-neighborhood-vanishes.html |title=Sit in This Chair, Go Back in Time; Barber Is Unchanged as Old Neighborhood Vanishes |last=Berger |first=Joseph |date=November 11, 2002 |work=The New York Times |page=1 |access-date=May 28, 2011}}</ref> was threatened with closure by a rent increase in May 2011<ref name="Berger2">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/05/13/nyregion/east-harlem-rent-tripling-barber-may-have-to-close-shop-after-60-years.html |title=East Harlem Rent Tripling, Barber May Have to Close Shop After 60 Years |last=Berger |first=Joseph |date=May 13, 2011 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=May 13, 2011}}</ref> but ultimately closed only in 2019 when Mr. Caponigro retired.<ref name="NYSDS">{{cite web |url=https://dos.ny.gov/news/new-york-secretary-state-robert-j-rodriguez-issues-proclamation-legendary-barber-and-promotes |title=New York Secretary of State Robert J. Rodriguez Issues Proclamation to Legendary Barber and Promotes Career Opportunities|date=October 26, 2022|website=dos.ny.gov}}</ref>

===Spanish Harlem===
{{redirect|Spanish Harlem|the song|Spanish Harlem (song)|the album by Ben E. King|Spanish Harlem (album)}}
[[Puerto Rican people|Puerto Rican]] and [[Latin America]]n migration after the [[First World War]]<ref name="fednyc">{{cite fednyc}}. p. 265-268</ref> established an enclave at the western portion of East Harlem – around [[110th Street (Manhattan)|110th Street]] and [[Lexington Avenue]] – which became known as "Spanish Harlem". The area slowly grew to encompass all of East Harlem, including Italian Harlem, as Italians moved out – to [[the Bronx]], [[Brooklyn]], [[Long Island]], [[upstate New York]], and [[New Jersey]] – and Puerto Ricans moved in during another wave of immigration in the 1940s and 1950s.<ref name=enc-nyc />

The newly dominant Puerto Rican population, which reached 63,000 in 1950, continued to define the neighborhood according to its needs, establishing [[bodega (store)|bodegas]] and [[botánica]]s as it expanded; by the 1930s<ref name=fednyc /> there was already an enclosed street market underneath the [[Park Avenue]] railroad viaduct between 111th and [[116th Street (Manhattan)|116th]] Streets, called "La Marqueta" ("The Market").<ref name=enc-nyc /> [[Catholic]] and [[Evangelical|evangelistic Protestant]] churches appeared in storefronts.<ref name=enc-nyc /> Although "Spanish Harlem" had been in use since at least the 1930s to describe the Latino enclave – along with "Italian Harlem" and "Negro Harlem"<ref>{{cite fednyc}}, p.253</ref> – the name began to be used to describe the entire East Harlem neighborhood by the 1950s. Later, the name "El Barrio" ("The Neighborhood") began to be used, especially by residents of the area.

===Decline===
In the 1950s and 1960s, large sections of East Harlem were leveled for [[urban renewal]] projects, and the neighborhood was one of the hardest hit areas in the 1960s and 1970s as New York City struggled with budget deficits, [[race riots]], [[White flight|urban flight]], gang warfare, drug abuse, crime and poverty. [[Tenements]] were crowded, poorly maintained, and frequent targets for arson. In 1969 and 1970, a regional chapter of the [[Young Lords]] which were reorganized from a neighborhood street gang in Chicago by [[Jose (Cha-Cha) Jimenez]], ran several programs including a Free Breakfast for Children and a Free Health Clinic to help Latino and poor families. The Young Lords came together with the [[Black Panthers]] and called for [[Puerto Rican independence movement|Puerto Rican independence]] and neighborhood empowerment.

===Recent history===
[[File:Sonder (45299154181).jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Looking north over East Harlem between [[Third Avenue|Third]] and [[Lexington Avenue|Lexington]] Avenues]]
By the beginning of the 21st century, East Harlem was a racially diverse neighborhood, with about a third of the population being Puerto Rican.<ref name=enc-nyc /> As it has been throughout its history, it is predominantly a [[working class in the United States|working-class]] neighborhood.<ref name=aia>{{cite aia5|page=548}}</ref>

Until 2006, property values in East Harlem climbed along with those in the rest of New York City, leading to gentrification and [[gentrification in the United States|changes to area demographics]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.businessinsider.com/east-harlem-gentrification-photos-2013-11 |title=Yuppies Are Moving into Notorious East Harlem |website=[[Business Insider]]|first=Daniel|last=Goodman |date=November 20, 2013 |access-date=November 20, 2013}}</ref>

On March 12, 2014, at 9:00 [[Eastern Daylight Time|EDT]], [[2014 East Harlem gas explosion|a large explosion]] and fire at 1644–1646 [[Park Avenue]] killed eight people and injured more than 70.<ref>[http://news.sky.com/story/1224778/explosion-and-building-collapse-in-new-york "New York Gas Explosion Kills Six People"] ''[[Sky News]]'' (March 13, 2014)</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Alcindor|first=Yamiche|author2=Doug Stanglin|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2014/03/13/east-harlem-explosion-gas-leak-bodies/6363235/ |title=8th body found in ruins of East Harlem buildings|newspaper=[[USA Today]]|date=March 13, 2014}} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170929064544/https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2014/03/13/east-harlem-explosion-gas-leak-bodies/6363235/ |date=September 29, 2017 }}.</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/03/13/nyregion/east-harlem-building-collapse.html?hp |title=At Least 3 Killed in Gas Blast on East Harlem Block; 2 Buildings Leveled |author=Santora, Marc |newspaper=The New York Times |date=March 12, 2014 |access-date=March 12, 2014}}</ref>

The ''[[New York Post]]'' listed one part of the neighborhood – the block of [[Lexington Avenue]] between East 123rd and 124th Streets – as one of "the most dangerous blocks in the city" because police crime statistics for 2015 showed that 19 assaults had taken place there, more than for any other city block. The ''Post'' also reported that there were, according to the Harlem Neighborhood Block Association, "22 drug-treatment programs, four homeless-service providers and four transitional-living facilities" in East Harlem.<ref>Balsamini, Dean (March 6, 2016) [https://nypost.com/2016/03/06/do-you-live-on-one-of-new-yorks-most-dangerous-blocks/ "Do you live on one of New York's most dangerous blocks?"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200914211547/https://nypost.com/2016/03/06/do-you-live-on-one-of-new-yorks-most-dangerous-blocks/ |date=September 14, 2020 }} ''[[New York Post]]''.</ref>

East Harlem has begun to feel the effects of [[gentrification]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.businessinsider.com/new-yorks-east-harlem-gentrification-photos-2013-9?op=1 |title=New York's East Harlem: Neighborhood Fighting To Keep Its Culture In The Face Of Gentrification |first=Daniel |last=Goodman |website=Business Insider |date=September 9, 2013 |access-date=April 12, 2016}}</ref> In February 2016, an article in ''The New York Times'' about "New York's Next Hot Neighborhoods" featured East Harlem as one of four such areas. A real-estate broker described it as "one of the few remaining areas in New York City where you can secure a good deal". The article mentioned new luxury developments, access to transportation, the opening of new retail stores, bars and restaurants, and national-brand stores beginning to appear on the outskirts of the neighborhood. Primarily, though, it was the cost of housing in comparison to the rest of Manhattan, which the article noted as the major factor.<ref name="hot">Higgins, Michelle (February 26, 2016) [https://www.nytimes.com/2016/02/28/realestate/new-yorks-next-hot-neighborhoods.html "New York's Next Hot Neighborhoods"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170929073223/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/02/28/realestate/new-yorks-next-hot-neighborhoods.html |date=September 29, 2017 }}. ''The New York Times''.</ref> Beginning in 2016, the New York City government was seeking to rezone East Harlem "to facilitate new residential, commercial, community facility, and manufacturing development".<ref>Staff (November 10, 2016), [https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/applicants/env-review/east-harlem/scoping-notice.pdf "East Harlem Scoping Notification"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170301141610/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/applicants/env-review/east-harlem/scoping-notice.pdf |date=March 1, 2017 }} [[New York City Department of City Planning]]</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/planning/applicants/scoping-documents.page#east-harlem |title=Scoping Documents Environmental Review – DCP |website=www1.nyc.gov}}</ref> The residents of the neighborhood generated a suggested zoning plan, the "East Harlem Neighborhood Plan", which was offered to the city in February 2017,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.eastharlemplan.nyc/ |title=East Harlem Neighborhood Plan |website=www.eastharlemplan.nyc}}</ref> but in August 2017 residents and the [[Manhattan Borough President]], [[Gale Brewer]], complained that the city had ignored their plan almost entirely.<ref>Solis, Gustavo (August 24, 2017) [https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20170824/east-harlem/el-barrio-rezoning-gale-brewer-mayor-bill-de-blasio "Mayor Ignoring Residents in East Harlem Rezoning Plan, Boro Prez Says"] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170907081030/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20170824/east-harlem/el-barrio-rezoning-gale-brewer-mayor-bill-de-blasio |date=September 7, 2017 }} ''[[DNAinfo]]''</ref>

In 2019, the oldest portion of the neighborhood, the blocks of [[111th Street (Manhattan)|East 111th]] through [[120th Street (Manhattan)|120th]] Streets between [[Park Avenue|Park]] and [[Pleasant Avenue|Pleasant]] Avenues, was listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]] as the East Harlem Historic District.<ref name="NRHP listing">{{cite web |title=Weekly List 20190712 |url=https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nationalregister/upload/weekly-list-2019-national-register-of-historic-places.pdf |publisher=[[U.S. National Park Service]] |date=July 12, 2019 |access-date=July 15, 2019}}</ref>

==Demographics==
[[File:Elbarrio116thLex.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|left|Storefronts at [[Lexington Avenue]] and [[116th Street (Manhattan)|116th Street]]]]
The [[New York City Department of City Planning]] classifies East Harlem into two neighborhood tabulation areas: East Harlem North and East Harlem South, divided along 115th Street.<ref>[https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/ntas.pdf New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181129141839/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/ntas.pdf |date=November 29, 2018 }}, Population Division - New York City Department of City Planning, February 2012. Accessed June 16, 2016.</ref> The two areas had a combined population of 115,921, an increase of 1,874 (1.4%) from the combined 114,047 in the [[2000 United States census|2000 Census]].<ref name="PLP5South"/>

=== 2010 census ===
Based on data from the [[2010 United States census]], the population of East Harlem North was 58,019, an increase of 871 (1.5%) from the 57,148 counted in 2000. Covering an area of {{cvt|573.94|acres}}, the neighborhood had a population density of {{cvt|101.1|PD/acre|PD/sqmi PD/sqkm}}.<ref name="PLP5South">[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf Table PL-P5 NTA: Total Population and Persons Per Acre – New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610175331/http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf |date=June 10, 2016 }}, Population Division – [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, February 2012. Accessed June 16, 2016.</ref> The racial makeup of the neighborhood was 6.8% (3,936) [[White (U.S. Census)|White]], 35.5% (20,625) [[African American (U.S. Census)|African American]], 0.2% (128) [[Native American (U.S. Census)|Native American]], 3.0% (1,766) [[Asian (U.S. Census)|Asian]], 0.0% (9) [[Pacific Islander (U.S. Census)|Pacific Islander]], 0.3% (185) from [[Race (United States Census)|other races]], and 1.3% (769) from two or more races. [[Hispanic (U.S. Census)|Hispanic]] or [[Latino (U.S. Census)|Latino]] of any race were 52.7% (30,601) of the population.<ref name="PLP3ASouth">[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p3a_nta.pdf Table PL-P3A NTA: Total Population by Mutually Exclusive Race and Hispanic Origin – New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610170733/http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p3a_nta.pdf |date=June 10, 2016 }}, Population Division – [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, March 29, 2011. Accessed June 14, 2016.</ref>

Based on data from the 2010 Census, the population of East Harlem South was 57,902, an increase of 1,003 (1.8%) from the 56,899 counted in 2000. Covering an area of {{cvt|389.41|acres}}, the neighborhood had a population density of {{cvt|148.7|PD/acre|PD/sqmi PD/sqkm}}.<ref name="PLP5South" /> The racial makeup of the neighborhood was 17.4% (10,072) White, 24.6% (14,227) African American, 0.2% (96) Native American, 8.3% (4,802) Asian, 0.1% (55) Pacific Islander, 0.4% (218) from other races, and 1.6% (933) from two or more races. Hispanic or Latino of any race were 47.5% (27,499) of the population.<ref name="PLP3ASouth" />

The most significant changes in the racial composition of East Harlem between 2000 and 2010 were the Asian population's increase by 109% (3,427), the White population's increase by 68% (5,689), and the Black population's decrease by 12% (4,625). Although more of the influx of Asian and White residents was in East Harlem South, the greatest percentage growth was in East Harlem North, while the Black population's decrease was evenly split. The Hispanic/Latino population also decreased by 4% (2,485), a decrease almost entirely concentrated in East Harlem South, where it fell from being the majority group to the plurality group. The small population of other races experienced a slight increase of 5% (132).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.urbanresearchmaps.org/plurality/files/RaceEthnic%20Change%20by%20Neighborhood%205-23-11.xls |title=Race / Ethnic Change by Neighborhood |publisher=Center for Urban Research, The Graduate Center, CUNY |date=May 23, 2011 |access-date=March 19, 2020 |format=Excel file}}</ref>

The entirety of [[Manhattan Community Board 11|Manhattan Community District 11]], which consists of East Harlem, [[Randall's Island]], and [[Ward's Island]], had 124,323 inhabitants as of [[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene|NYC Health]]'s 2018 Community Health Profile, with an average life expectancy of 77.3 years.<ref name="CHP2018">{{cite web |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/data/2018chp-mn11.pdf |title=East Harlem (Including East Harlem, Randalls Island and Wards Island) |date=2018 |website=nyc.gov |publisher=NYC Health |access-date=March 2, 2019 |quote=East Harlem's average life expectancy is 3.9 years shorter than NYC overall. - 77.3 Life Expectancy}}</ref>{{Rp|2, 20}} This is 3.9 years lower than the median life expectancy of 81.2 for all New York City neighborhoods.<ref name=":21">{{cite web |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/tcny/community-health-assessment-plan.pdf |title=2016-2018 Community Health Assessment and Community Health Improvement Plan: Take Care New York 2020 |date=2016 |website=[[government of New York City|nyc.gov]] |publisher=[[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene]] |access-date=September 8, 2017 |archive-date=September 9, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170909004755/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/tcny/community-health-assessment-plan.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>{{Rp|53 (PDF p. 84)}} Most residents are children and middle-aged adults: 21% are between the ages of 0–17, while 33% are between 25 and 44, and 23% are between 45 and 64. The ratio of college-aged and elderly residents was lower, at 10% and 13% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|2}}

As of 2017, the median [[household income]] in Community District 11 was $36,770.<ref name="CB11PUMA">{{cite web |url=https://censusreporter.org/profiles/79500US3603804-nyc-manhattan-community-district-11-east-harlem-puma-ny/ |title=NYC-Manhattan Community District 11--East Harlem PUMA, NY |access-date=July 17, 2018 |archive-date=March 25, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190325163107/https://censusreporter.org/profiles/79500US3603804-nyc-manhattan-community-district-11-east-harlem-puma-ny/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 2018, an estimated 23% of Community District 11 residents lived in [[poverty]], compared to 14% in all of Manhattan and 20% in all of New York City. One in nine residents (11%) were unemployed, compared to 7% in Manhattan and 9% in New York City. Rent burden, or the percentage of residents who have difficulty paying their rent, is 48% in Community District 11, compared to the boroughwide and citywide rates of 45% and 51% respectively. Based on this calculation, {{as of|2018|lc=y}}, Community District 11 was considered to be [[gentrification|gentrifying]]: according to the Community Health Profile, the district was low-income in 1990 and has seen above-median rent growth up to 2010.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|7}}

===Ethnic groups===
Community District 11 is a mostly low to middle income area. It is made up of first and second generation [[Puerto Ricans]], [[Dominican Americans]], [[Cuban Americans]], [[African Americans]], [[Italian Americans]], [[Asian Americans]], [[West Indian Americans|Caribbean Americans]] and a growing population of [[Mexican Americans]] and [[Salvadoran Americans]] and other [[Central America]]n immigrants. ====Asian residents====
The number of [[Asian Americans|Asians]] in East Harlem more than doubled between 2000 and 2010, largely due to Chinese people moving to East Harlem. Increasing rents in [[Chinatown, Manhattan|Lower Manhattan's Chinatown]] and the city's other Chinatowns led many Chinese New Yorkers to apply for various [[affordable housing]] programs; some applicants were given units in East Harlem after their housing applications were approved. Mitchell Lama's Franklin Plaza in the neighborhood has been well reported with having an influx of Chinese residents. Advocates have been calling for Chinese language services to be available in the community centers to accommodate the growing number of Chinese residents in the area. In 2000, the Chinese population in the northern portion was less than one percent, but by 2010, it has gone up to three percent. In the southern part, it rose from 4.6% to 8.4%.<ref name="Mays 2011">{{cite news |last=Mays |first=Jeff |url=http://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20110803/harlem/east-harlem-tries-serve-huge-influx-of-chinese-residents |title=East Harlem Tries to Serve Huge Influx of Chinese Residents |newspaper=[[DNAinfo]] |date=August 3, 2011 |access-date=September 19, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130224002454/http://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20110803/harlem/east-harlem-tries-serve-huge-influx-of-chinese-residents |archive-date=February 24, 2013}}</ref><ref name="Barron 2013">{{cite news |last=Barron |first=Laignee |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/chinese-population-climbs-200-harlem-east-harlem-10-yrs-article-1.947039 |title=Chinese population climbs 200% in Harlem and East Harlem over 10 yrs |newspaper=[[New York Daily News]] |date=August 8, 2011 |access-date=September 19, 2012}}</ref><ref name="APA 2012">{{cite web |url=http://www.apaforprogress.org/chinese-american-population-harlem-nyc-surges |title=Chinese American Population in Harlem NYC Surges |publisher=apaforprogress.org |access-date=September 19, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131109010909/http://www.apaforprogress.org/chinese-american-population-harlem-nyc-surges |archive-date=November 9, 2013}}</ref> Although their population is still very small in the district, they have gotten a lot media attention over their presence in the area's affordable housing developments.

Elderly Asian residents have reported feeling isolated in East Harlem due to their limited English proficiency and lack of resources. Some of the Asian residents have experienced racially motivated harassment; for example, Chinese American senior [[Killing of Yao Pan Ma|Yao Pan Ma]] was beaten to death in East Harlem in 2021. In 2023, a New York University journalist conducted an interview with the Chinese speaking elders living in [[New York City Housing Authority]] (NYCHA)'s [[George Washington Carver Houses]] reflecting on the difficulties they experienced in East Harlem.<ref>{{cite AV media |date=August 25, 2023 |title=Out Of Place: Asian Seniors in East Harlem Public Housing |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qHBO-Rx54N8 |publisher=Aria Young |access-date=May 27, 2026 |via=YouTube}}</ref><ref>{{cite AV media |date=April 25, 2021 |title=Group To March From Washington Heights To Site Of Brutal Attack On Asian Man In East Harlem |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3732JZ0-X5I |publisher=CBS New York |access-date=May 27, 2026 |via=YouTube}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.aafe.org/aafe-in-east-harlem-providing-accessible-services-building-community/ |title=AAFE in East Harlem: Providing Accessible Services, Building Community |website=Asian Americans for Equality |access-date=May 27, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Murphy |first=Colum |date=April 11, 2019 |url=https://chinarrative.substack.com/p/chinese-of-fifth-avenue-east-harlem |title=Chinese of Fifth Avenue: East Harlem |access-date=May 27, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Yee |first=Amy |date=February 3, 2023 |url=https://www.carterburdennetwork.org/news-blog/2023/2/3/bloomberg-why-asian-americans-are-moving-to-nycs-east-harlem |title=Why Asian Americans Are Moving to NYC's East Harlem |work=Bloomberg |via=Carter Burden Network |access-date=May 27, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=January 9, 2022 |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/yao-pan-ma-brutally-beaten-in-east-harlem-dies-from-injuries-months-later/ |title=61-Year-Old Asian Man Brutally Beaten In East Harlem Dies From Injuries Months Later |work=CBS New York |access-date=May 27, 2026}}</ref>

===Social issues===
Social problems, including concentrated poverty, homelessness, overcrowding, substandard housing, language barriers, food insecurity, teen pregnancy, obesity, crime, drug addiction, dropping out of school, and low rates of advanced educational attainment, have long plagued the area. Although crime rates have dropped from the historically high numbers during the [[crack epidemic]], East Harlem suffers from a high [[violent crime]] rate, especially in the 25th Precinct above 115th Street. In 2021, the 25th Precinct had the second-highest rates of [[felony assault]] and robbery, the 16th-highest rate of rape, and the highest rate of murder out of the [[New York Police Department]]'s 77 precincts.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://maps.nyc.gov/crime/ |title=NYC Crime Map |access-date=March 21, 2020 |website=www.nyc.gov |publisher=New York Police Department}}</ref>

East Harlem has the highest concentration of shelters and facilities in Manhattan, with eight [[homeless shelter]]s, 36 drug and alcohol treatment facilities and 37 [[mental health]] treatment facilities. It also has the highest jobless rate in the entire city, as well as the city's second-highest cumulative [[HIV/AIDS|AIDS]] rate. The [[asthma]] rate is also five times higher than national levels.<ref name="nyc.gov" /> The neighborhood also suffers from a high poverty rate.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://home2.nyc.gov/html/ceo/images/misc/chart_5.jpg |title=Archived copy |access-date=March 6, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080627153857/http://home2.nyc.gov/html/ceo/images/misc/chart_5.jpg |archive-date=June 27, 2008}}</ref> [[Union Settlement Association]] is one of the neighborhood's largest social service agencies, reaching more than 13,000 people annually at 17 locations throughout East Harlem, through a range of programs, including early childhood education, youth development, senior services, job training, the arts, [[adult education]], nutrition, counseling, a [[farmers' market]], community development, and neighborhood cultural events.

==Housing==
East Harlem is dominated by [[Public housing in the United States|public housing]] complexes of various types, with a high concentration of older [[tenement]] buildings between these developments. The neighborhood contains the second-highest concentration of public housing in the United States, behind [[Brownsville, Brooklyn]].<ref name="Mays 2011 2">{{cite web |last=Mays |first=Jeff |url=http://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20110414/harlem/lowincome-parents-worry-cuts-childcare-will-force-them-out-of-work |title=Low-Income Parents Worry Cuts to Childcare Will Force Them Out of Work – DNAinfo.com New York |publisher=Dnainfo.com |date=April 14, 2011 |access-date=September 19, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121008003622/http://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20110414/harlem/lowincome-parents-worry-cuts-childcare-will-force-them-out-of-work |archive-date=October 8, 2012}}</ref> The total land area is {{cvt|1.54|sqmi|km2}}.<ref name=communityboard>{{cite web |url=http://www.nyc.gov/html/dcp/pdf/lucds/mn11profile.pdf |title=Manhattan Community Board 11 |date=December 2007 |work=nyc.gov |publisher=New York City Department of Planning |access-date=January 3, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130928060104/http://www.nyc.gov/html/dcp/pdf/lucds/mn11profile.pdf |archive-date=September 28, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.census.gov |title=Census Tract 240 |work=[[United States Census Bureau]] |publisher=US Census Bureau |access-date=January 3, 2009}}</ref>

After a wave of [[arson]] ravaged the low income communities of New York City throughout the 1970s, many of the residential structures in East Harlem were left seriously damaged or destroyed. By the late 1970s, the city began to rehabilitate many abandoned tenement style buildings and designate them as [[low income housing]]. Despite recent [[gentrification]] of the neighborhood, large numbers of apartment buildings have been deliberately kept vacant by their owners. Although the businesses on the ground floor are retained, landlords do not want to have the trouble involved in residential tenants. In some cases, landlords are waiting for a revived economy, warehousing the apartments so that they can rent them later at a higher rent.<ref name="Sealed Apartments">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/10/31/nyregion/east-harlem-landlords-keep-apartments-sealed-up.html |title=East Harlem Landlords Keep Apartments Sealed Up |date=October 31, 2011 |work=The New York Times |access-date=October 31, 2011}}</ref>

In 2007, a survey of Manhattan's buildings found that 1,723 were significantly vacant, three-quarters of them north of [[96th Street (Manhattan)|96th Street]]. A 1998 survey found that one-quarter of low-rise residential buildings on avenues or major cross streets in East Harlem had sealed-up residential floors, despite having commercial businesses on the ground floor.<ref name="Sealed Apartments" />

==Police and crime==
[[File:NYPD 25 Pct E119 jeh.JPG|thumb|upright=1.1|[[New York Police Department|NYPD]]'s 25th Precinct station house]]
East Harlem is served by two precincts of the [[New York City Police Department]]  (NYPD).<ref>{{cite web |title=Find Your Precinct and Sector - NYPD |website=www.nyc.gov |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/find-your-precinct.page |access-date=March 3, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author=Feeney, Michael J. |url=http://articles.nydailynews.com/2012-05-11/news/31672547_1_violence-east-harlem-community-leaders |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130130134524/http://articles.nydailynews.com/2012-05-11/news/31672547_1_violence-east-harlem-community-leaders |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 30, 2013 |title=Plea for peace in East Harlem |newspaper=[[New York Daily News]] |date=May 11, 2012 |access-date=September 19, 2012}}</ref> The area north of [[116th Street (Manhattan)|116th Street]] is served by the 25th Precinct, located at 120 East 119th Street,<ref name="NYPD 25th Precinct">{{cite web |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/25th-precinct.page |title=NYPD – 25th Precinct |website=www.nyc.gov |publisher=[[New York City Police Department]] |access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref> while the area south of 116th Street is served by the 23rd Precinct, located at 164 East 102nd Street.<ref name="NYPD 23rd Precinct">{{cite web |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/23rd-precinct.page |title=NYPD – 23rd Precinct |website=www.nyc.gov |publisher=[[New York City Police Department]] |access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref>

The 25th Precinct has a lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with crimes across all categories having decreased by 72.1% between 1990 and 2024. The precinct reported 8 murders, 16 rapes, 257 robberies, 478 felony assaults, 108 burglaries, 490 grand larcenies, and 109 grand larcenies auto in 2024.<ref name="NYPD 25th Precinct CS">{{cite web |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-025pct.pdf |title=25th Precinct CompStat Report |website=www.nyc.gov |publisher=[[New York City Police Department]] |access-date=March 20, 2020}}</ref> Of the five major violent felonies (murder, rape, felony assault, robbery, and burglary), the 25th Precinct had a rate of 1,340 crimes per 100,000 residents in 2019, compared to the boroughwide average of 632 crimes per 100,000 and the citywide average of 572 crimes per 100,000.<ref name="crime map"/><ref name="sevenmajorfelonies">{{cite web |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/analysis_and_planning/historical-crime-data/seven-major-felony-offenses-2000-2019.pdf |title=Citywide Seven Major Felony Offenses 2000-2019 |publisher=[[New York Police Department]] |access-date=March 23, 2020 |website=www.nyc.gov}}</ref><ref name="sevenmajorfeloniesbyprecinct"/>

==Health==
[[File:SinaiMed crop.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|[[Mount Sinai Hospital (Manhattan)|Mount Sinai Medical Center]] as seen from [[Central Park]]]]
{{As of|2018}}, [[preterm birth]]s and births to teenage mothers in East Harlem are higher than the city average. In East Harlem, there were 108 preterm births per 1,000 live births (compared to 87 per 1,000 citywide), and 10.8 teenage births per 1,000 live births (compared to 19.3 per 1,000 citywide), though the teenage birth rate was based on a small sample size.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|11}} East Harlem has a low population of residents who are [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|uninsured]]. In 2018, this population of uninsured residents was estimated to be 3%, less than the citywide rate of 12%, though this was based on a small sample size.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|14}}

The concentration of [[particulates|fine particulate matter]], the deadliest type of [[air pollution|air pollutant]], in East Harlem is {{cvt|0.0082|mg/m3|oz/ft3}}, more than the city average.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|9}} Eighteen percent of East Harlem residents are [[Smoking|smokers]], which is more than the city average of 14% of residents being smokers.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} In East Harlem, 28% of residents are [[Obesity|obese]], 17% are [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetic]], and 34% have [[hypertension|high blood pressure]]—compared to the citywide averages of 24%, 11%, and 28% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|16}} In addition, 23% of children are obese, compared to the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|12}}

Eighty-four percent of residents eat some fruits and vegetables every day, which is lower than the city's average of 87%. In 2018, 76% of residents described their health as "good", "very good", or "excellent", less than the city's average of 78%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} For every supermarket in East Harlem, there are 17 [[convenience store|bodegas]].<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|10}}

[[Metropolitan Hospital Center]] and [[Mount Sinai Hospital (Manhattan)|Mount Sinai Hospital]] are both located in southern East Harlem. ===Fresh food===
[[File:Super Associated East Harlem 1968 2nd Av 101 St jeh.jpg|thumb|left|upright=1.1|[[Associated Supermarkets]] on East 101st Street]]
A lack of access to healthy food causes serious hardships to citizens of East Harlem, a neighborhood which is considered to be a [[food desert]]. According to an April 2008 report prepared by the [[New York City Department of City Planning]], East Harlem is an area of the city with the highest levels of diet-related diseases due to limited opportunities for citizens to purchase fresh foods.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nyc.gov/html/dcp/html/supermarket/index.shtml |title=Socioeconomic & Housing – Going to Market: New York City's Neighborhood Grocery Store and Supermarket Shortage |publisher=Nyc.gov |access-date=September 19, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121016051109/http://www.nyc.gov/html/dcp/html/supermarket/index.shtml |archive-date=October 16, 2012}}</ref>

With a high population density and a lack of nearby [[supermarkets]], the neighborhood has little access to fresh fruit and vegetables and a low consumption of fresh foods. Citizens of East Harlem are likely to buy food from grocery stores that have a limited supply of fruits and vegetables, which are often of poor quality and generally more expensive than the same products sold at supermarkets. Compared to the [[Upper East Side]], supermarkets in Harlem are 30% less common.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.nyc.gov/portal/site/nycgov/menuitem.c0935b9a57bb4ef3daf2f1c701c789a0/index.jsp?pageID=mayor_press_release&catID=1194&doc_name=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.nyc.gov%2Fhtml%2Fom%2Fhtml%2F2007b%2Fpr467-07.html&cc=unused1978&rc=1194&ndi=1 |title=Mayor Bloomberg and Speaker Quinn Announce Green Cart Legislation to Improve Access to Fresh Fruits and Vegetables in Neighborhoods With Greatest Need |publisher=NYC.gov |date=December 18, 2007 |access-date=September 19, 2012 |archive-date=October 16, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121016182646/http://www.nyc.gov/portal/site/nycgov/menuitem.c0935b9a57bb4ef3daf2f1c701c789a0/index.jsp?pageID=mayor_press_release&catID=1194&doc_name=http://www.nyc.gov/html/om/html/2007b/pr467-07.html&cc=unused1978&rc=1194&ndi=1 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Without access to affordable produce and meats, East Harlem residents have difficulty eating a healthy diet, which contributes to high rates of [[obesity]] and [[diabetes]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=American Journal of Preventive Medicine – Supermarkets, Other Food Stores, and Obesity: The Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Study |date=March 10, 2006 |doi=10.1016/j.amepre.2005.11.003 |volume=30 |journal=American Journal of Preventive Medicine |pages=333–339 |pmid=16530621 |last1=Morland |first1=K |last2=Diez Roux |first2=AV |last3=Wing |first3=S |issue=4 |hdl=2027.42/57754 |url=https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/2027.42/57754/1/Supermarkets%20other%20food%20stores%20and%20obesity.pdf|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

In 2011, Manhattan Borough President [[Scott Stringer]] announced a program which would send Veggie Vans to East Harlem senior centers and housing projects.<ref>{{cite web |last=Resto-Montero |first=Gabriela |date=February 8, 2011 |url=http://www.dnainfo.com/20110208/harlem/veggie-vans-slated-sell-fresh-produce-east-harlem |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120724062246/http://www.dnainfo.com/20110208/harlem/veggie-vans-slated-sell-fresh-produce-east-harlem |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 24, 2012 |title=Veggie Vans Slated to Sell Fresh Produce in East Harlem |work=DNAinfo |access-date=September 19, 2012}}</ref> In 2012, [[Whole Foods Market|Whole Foods]] announced two uptown locations, one being on [[125th Street (Manhattan)|125th Street]] and [[Lenox Avenue]], the other on the Upper East Side.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10000872396390443854204578061032529621890 |title=Whole Foods Plans New Stores for Harlem, Upper East Side |newspaper=The Wall Street Journal |date=October 16, 2012 |access-date=October 16, 2012 |last1=Kusisto |first1=Laura }}</ref> In 2010, [[Aldi|Aldi's Grocery]] opened at the [[East River Plaza]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.eastriverplaza.com/homepage.html |title=East River Plaza |publisher=East River Plaza |access-date=April 9, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150503165641/http://www.eastriverplaza.com/homepage.html |archive-date=May 3, 2015 |url-status=dead}}</ref> located at E. 117th St. and the [[FDR Drive]], providing access to affordable food for East Harlem's residents. In 2013, a new Super FI Emperior Grocery store opened up in East Harlem on 103rd Street and [[Lexington Avenue]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://thesource.com/2013/07/26/super-fi-opens-in-harlem/ |title=Super Fi Emporium Opens In Harlem |date=July 26, 2013 |publisher=The Source |access-date=July 26, 2013}}</ref>

==Education==
{{Main|Education in Harlem}}
[[File:Tito Puente PS117 2095 2nd Av 240 E109 St jeh.jpg|thumb|left|upright=1.1|A school named after musician [[Tito Puente]]]]
East Harlem generally has a lower rate of college-educated residents than the rest of the city {{as of|2018|lc=y}}. While 38% have a college education or higher, 25% have less than a high school education and 37% are high school graduates or have some college education. By contrast, 64% of Manhattan residents and 43% of city residents have a college education or higher.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} The percentage of East Harlem students excelling in math rose from 25% in 2000 to 51% in 2011, and reading achievement increased from 33% to 39% during the same time period.<ref name=":17">{{cite web |url=http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/MN_11_11.pdf |title=East Harlem – MN 11 |date=2011 |publisher=[[Furman Center for Real Estate and Urban Policy]] |access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref>

East Harlem's rate of elementary school student absenteeism is higher than the rest of New York City. In East Harlem, 30% of elementary school students missed 20 or more days per [[school year]], more than the citywide average of 20%.<ref name=":21" />{{Rp|24 (PDF p. 55)}}<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} Additionally, 67% of high school students in East Harlem graduate on time, less than the citywide average of 75%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}}

As in other parts of the city, some schools require students pass through [[metal detector]]s and swipe ID cards to enter school buildings.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://harlemworldmag.com/2010/10/10/east-harlem-harlem-ny/ |title=East Harlem, Harlem, NY | |publisher=Harlemworldmag.com |date=October 10, 2010 |access-date=September 19, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120519231006/http://harlemworldmag.com/2010/10/10/east-harlem-harlem-ny/ |archive-date=May 19, 2012}}</ref>

The [[Harlem River]] separates [[the Bronx]] and Manhattan, necessitating several spans between the two New York City boroughs. Three free bridges connect East Harlem and the Bronx: the [[Willis Avenue Bridge]] (for northbound traffic only), [[Third Avenue Bridge (New York City)|Third Avenue Bridge]] (for southbound traffic only), and [[Madison Avenue Bridge]]. In East Harlem, the [[Wards Island Bridge]], also known as the 103rd Street Footbridge, connects Manhattan with [[Wards Island]]. The [[Triborough Bridge]] (officially the Robert F. Kennedy Bridge) is a complex of three separate bridges that offers connections between [[Queens]], East Harlem, and the Bronx.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://web.mta.info/bandt/html/rfk.html |title=Robert F. Kennedy Bridge |date=December 30, 2010 |publisher=Mta.info |access-date=February 2, 2013}}</ref>

Public transportation service is provided by the [[Metropolitan Transportation Authority]]. The [[New York City Subway]]'s [[IRT Lexington Avenue Line]] runs through East Harlem, with an express station at [[125th Street (IRT Lexington Avenue Line)|125th Street]] (served by the {{NYCS trains|Lexington|type=route}}) as well as local stations at the [[116th Street (IRT Lexington Avenue Line)|116th Street]], [[110th Street (IRT Lexington Avenue Line)|110th Street]], [[103rd Street (IRT Lexington Avenue Line)|103rd Street]], and [[96th Street (IRT Lexington Avenue Line)|96th Street]] (served by the {{NYCS trains|Lexington local day|type=route}}). There is also a [[Second Avenue Subway]] station at [[96th Street (Second Avenue Subway)|96th Street]] on the {{NYCS trains|Second header|type=route}}.<ref>{{NYCS const|map}}</ref> [[MTA Regional Bus Operations]]{{'}} {{NYC bus link|M15|M15 SBS|M35|M60 SBS|M96|M98|M101|M102|M103|M106|M116}} and {{NYC bus link|M125}} bus routes serve East Harlem as well.<ref>{{Cite NYC bus map|M}}</ref> [[Metro-North Railroad]] has a [[commuter rail]] station at [[Harlem–125th Street (Metro-North station)|Harlem–125th Street]], serving trains to the [[Lower Hudson Valley]] and [[Connecticut]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://web.mta.info/mnr/html/mnrmap.htm |title=Metro-North Railroad Map |date=2017 |publisher=[[Metropolitan Transportation Authority]] |access-date=May 14, 2017}}</ref>
